consumedBy.note: `module` is exactly a LearningModuleDefinition and nothing else. JSON.parse(file).module casts cleanly, and every key inside it — including each card's — is one the format declares. Everything this file adds for authoring lives outside `module`, so the player never sees a field it does not know.

module.title: Nailed to the Post
module.subtitle: Three minutes. Everything the constable can ask you is in here.

body: Boston, 14 August 1765. You run printed sheets through this town for Mercer's Press and nobody looks twice.
Today one sheet matters. Read it before you carry it.

beats.text: Boston, the fourteenth of August, 1765. You run printed sheets through this town for Mercer's Press, and nobody looks at you twice.
Today one sheet matters. Read it before you carry it. Everything the constable can ask you is in the next three minutes.

body: Britain's war with France ended in 1763. Britain won it, and came out owing more than it had ever owed before — with an army still to pay for in America.
Parliament looked across the Atlantic and decided the colonies should pay a share of that debt. That decision is why a tax is suddenly reaching into Boston.
Keep the order straight: the debt came first, and the tax is Parliament's answer to it, not the other way round.

beats.text: Britain's war with France ended in 1763. Britain won it. But the war left it owing more than ever before. And there was still an army to pay for here in America.
Parliament looked across the Atlantic and decided the colonies should pay a share of that debt. That decision is why a tax is suddenly reaching into Boston.
Keep the order straight. The debt came first. The tax is Parliament's answer to it, not the other way round.

visuals.alt: Oil painting of the dying General Wolfe surrounded by officers on the battlefield at Quebec.
visuals.title: The Death of General Wolfe
visuals.caption: A later depiction: Benjamin West painted this in 1770 of an event of 1759. It is history painting, not documentary evidence — the war it recalls is the war that left Britain in debt.

check.prompt: After 1763, why did Parliament decide to raise revenue from the colonies?
check.reinforcement: The war left the debt; an army still had to be paid for in America; Parliament decided the colonies should share that cost.

correctOption.text: The war left Britain deep in debt, with an army still to keep in America, and Parliament decided the colonies should share that cost.
correctOption.feedback: Right. Debt and defence came first, and the tax is Parliament's answer to the bill.

distractorPool.text: The new stamp tax was itself what had put Britain into debt.
distractorPool.feedback: That reverses the order. The debt came first, from the war; the tax is how Parliament pays it down, not its cause.

distractorPool.text: The colonies had fallen years behind on taxes they already owed the Crown, and the Act was merely the machinery to collect everything that was overdue.
distractorPool.feedback: No. There were no such earlier taxes to fall behind on. The money was for the war debt and the cost of the army.

distractorPool.text: Parliament meant to punish Boston's merchants for smuggling goods past the customs house during the war.
distractorPool.feedback: No. The Act raised money; it was not a penalty. The brief traced it to war debt and an army to pay for, not to smuggling.

distractorPool.text: London's own merchants and the King's household were the ones meant to pay it down.
distractorPool.feedback: The wrong payer. Parliament decided the colonies should supply part of it, not people back in Britain.

distractorPool.text: Britain had just won new land in the war and wanted the colonists to go and settle it.
distractorPool.feedback: Land is not a bill. The Act raised revenue against the war debt; it did not fund settlement.

distractorPool.text: Every part of the empire was being taxed the same way, and the colonies were simply included.
distractorPool.feedback: Not so. The measure reached into the colonies in particular, to raise a revenue there against the war debt.

body: The tax has a shape, and the shape is the thing to learn. From 1 November, printed paper and legal paper must carry a stamp that somebody has paid for.

Inside it: newspapers, handbills, deeds, court papers, licences, even playing cards. Outside it: a bolt of cloth, a barrel of nails, a letter you wrote out by hand yourself. Ordinary goods are not the target.
Which is why the shop you run for is where this lands hardest. A printer's entire trade is the one thing being taxed.

beats.text: The tax has a shape, and that shape is the thing to learn. From the first of November, printed paper and legal paper must carry a stamp that someone has paid for.
It falls on newspapers, handbills, deeds, court papers, licences, even playing cards. It leaves out the ordinary things. A bolt of cloth, a barrel of nails, a letter in your own hand.
Which is why the shop you run for is where this lands hardest. A printer's whole trade is the one thing being taxed.

visuals.alt: Printed page of the 1765 Stamp Act with the Act's title and opening clauses set in period type.
visuals.title: The Stamp Act, 1765
visuals.caption: A primary source: a printed page of the Act itself, passed 22 March 1765. This is the law the sheet in your hand is fighting.

check.prompt: Come the first of November, which single item on a Boston shop's counter must carry the Crown's paid stamp?
check.reinforcement: The stamp falls on printed and legal paper, from the first of November. Ordinary goods and a letter written in your own hand stay outside it.

correctOption.text: The printed newspaper stacked on the counter.
correctOption.feedback: Yes. The line is drawn around printed and legal paper, and a newspaper sits squarely inside it.

distractorPool.text: A bolt of imported cloth, since it is sold from the very same counter.
distractorPool.feedback: No. Being sold in a shop does not put a thing inside the Act; being printed or legal paper does.

distractorPool.text: A barrel of nails from the chandler, because the Act reaches everything a shop trades.
distractorPool.feedback: No. Ordinary goods stay outside the Act. It is not a tax on trade; it is a tax on paper.

distractorPool.text: A private letter written and sealed in a woman's own hand.
distractorPool.feedback: No. Being paper is not the test. A letter in your own hand stays outside the Act; a printed sheet sits inside it.

distractorPool.text: Any goods shipped in from Britain, though nothing that was made here in Boston.
distractorPool.feedback: No. The Act turns on printed and legal paper, not on where a good was made or shipped from.

distractorPool.text: The hard silver in the till, since the stamp duty has to be settled in coin.
distractorPool.feedback: No. That the duty is paid in coin does not make the coin the thing taxed; the tax is on the paper.

distractorPool.text: Nothing in particular yet, since the Act passed back in the spring and so already falls on the whole shop alike.
distractorPool.feedback: No. The duty does not begin until the first of November, and even then it reaches paper, not the whole shop.

body: Boston does elect people — its own town meeting, its own representatives in the Massachusetts assembly. Those men could tax this town tomorrow.
Boston elects nobody in Parliament. Not one member. And Parliament is what laid this tax.

The claim underneath your sheet is this: a tax may be laid only by a body the taxed people chose. So the complaint is not the price — the town would say the same if the stamp cost a farthing. The complaint is who laid it.
London answers that Parliament speaks for every subject, voted for or not. Boston's reply is short: we chose none of you. A lawful vote by men we never picked is still not consent.

beats.text: Boston does elect people. It has its own town meeting, and its own members in the Massachusetts assembly. Those men could tax this town tomorrow.
But Boston elects nobody in Parliament. Not one member. And Parliament is the body that laid this tax.

The claim under your sheet is simple. A tax may be laid only by a body the taxed people chose. So the quarrel is not really the price. The town would say the same if the stamp cost a farthing. What it objects to is who laid it.
London answers that Parliament speaks for every subject, chosen or not. Boston's reply is short. We chose none of you. A lawful vote by men we never picked is still not consent.

visuals.alt: Engraved harbour view of Boston with British warships and lines of troops landing at the Long Wharf.
visuals.title: A View of Part of the Town of Boston, and the Landing of Troops, 1768
visuals.caption: A primary source: Paul Revere's engraving of British troops landing at Boston on 1 October 1768. It shows the town whose consent is in dispute — and what force behind a law without it looks like. Note the engraving postdates the 1765 module date.

check.prompt: What is Boston's actual objection to the Stamp Act?
check.reinforcement: Boston elects local bodies but no members of Parliament; it objects that a Parliament it never chose has no consent to tax it. The quarrel is over consent, not price.

correctOption.text: Boston elects its own town bodies but no members of Parliament, so it denies that a body it never chose may tax it.
correctOption.feedback: Right. The issue is who laid the tax, and whether the taxed people chose them, not what it costs.

distractorPool.text: The stamp costs too much, and Boston would take it at a lower price.
distractorPool.feedback: No. Boston would object even at a farthing. The complaint is who laid the tax, not what it costs.

distractorPool.text: Boston would accept the very same tax if the King laid it instead of Parliament.
distractorPool.feedback: No. Consent turns on whether Boston chose the body, and it chose the King's officers no more than Parliament.

distractorPool.text: Boston has no elected government of any kind and is demanding that one be created.
distractorPool.feedback: No. Boston already elects a town meeting and assembly. What it lacks is a voice in Parliament, the body that laid this tax.

distractorPool.text: The officials Parliament sends to collect the stamp are corrupt and grasping, and honest men in the same posts would satisfy the town.
distractorPool.feedback: No. Fairness is not the point. A tax needs the consent of people Boston elected, however upright the taxers are.

distractorPool.text: Parliament sits too far across the ocean to govern the affairs of Boston well.
distractorPool.feedback: No. Distance is not the argument. Boston would reject a member it never elected even if he lived on Milk Street.

distractorPool.text: The Act was pushed through Parliament in the wrong legal form and without the proper readings, so the town holds it simply void and of no binding effect.
distractorPool.feedback: No. The Act was passed by a lawful vote; Boston's ground is that a lawful vote by men it never chose is still not consent.

body: Three facts, one chain: a war left a debt, the debt produced a policy of raising money in America, and the policy produced the stamp.
Parliament wrote that much into the Act.

excerpt.title: The Stamp Act
lines: …it is just and necessary, that provision be made for raising a further revenue… in America, towards defraying the said expences…

beats.text: Three facts, one chain. A war left a debt. The debt produced a policy of raising money in America. And that policy produced the stamp.
Parliament wrote that much into the Act itself. It called it just and necessary that provision be made for raising a further revenue in America.

visuals.alt: Satirical engraving of a mock funeral procession carrying a small coffin labelled for the repealed Stamp Act along a wharf lined with bales of goods.
visuals.title: The Repeal, or the Funeral of Miss Ame-Stamp
visuals.caption: Period art: a 1766 London satirical print marking the Act's repeal — the argument in your hand, one year on. Contemporary comment, not documentary record.

body: Nail your sheet beside the Crown's notice at the public pump, before the constable papers over the board.
He will be standing there when you finish, and he will ask you what you think you know.

readingRateWpm.basis: Hasbrouck & Tindal (2017) oral reading fluency norms put the grade-8 spring 50th percentile at 151 words correct per minute. Silent reading of unfamiliar informational prose on a screen runs at or a little below that for this age, so 140 wpm is the planning rate and 120/160 bracket it. The card windows are sized against 140.

excerptRateWpm.basis: Period statutory English at half the modern-prose rate. A 24-word clause of 1765 legal syntax is not a 24-word sentence of ours, and pretending otherwise is how a three-minute module becomes four.

budget.note: Per-card and whole-deck arithmetic is recomputed from these strings by verify.mjs; the table in README.md is that script's output, not a hand tally.

windowRecut.why: Mission-Slate §4.7 sized its six windows before the cards had prose in them. Written out, the representation card needs about fifty seconds and not forty: it carries three propositions, the positive consent principle, and the answer to Parliament's speaks-for-everyone claim, and six of the eighteen duel items draw on it. The seconds come from the two frame cards and the stamp card, which came in under. The deck still totals exactly 180 and no window is shorter than its card's measured reading time.
windowRecut.slateFollowUp: §4.7's table still prints the old windows. Whoever next edits that section should copy the authored column across; this file is the content and that table is now a summary of it.

reinstated.content: The cost of keeping an army in America — 'with an army still to pay for in America', on the postwar card.
reinstated.wasExcluded: Mission-Slate §4.9's third verification note recorded that the retired multiple-choice item K1 graded this clause while the module taught it nowhere, and closed it on the rule that nothing may be graded that is taught nowhere.
reinstated.whyItIsBackIn: The capstone serves STAAR.2018MAY.G8SS.05, the only released TEA item on postwar revenue, and TEA's keyed option is 'To recover the cost of defending the colonies'. The item almost certainly discriminates on cost-recovery rather than on defence — its other three options are Britain spending rather than Britain recouping — but 'almost certainly' is not what should stand between a student and the concept's only item with real provenance. Seven words remove the doubt and honour §4.9's rule in the direction it always allowed: teach it, then grade it.
reinstated.costInSeconds: Zero. The seven words are paid for by tightening the sentence directly below them — 'Keep the order straight, because the order is the whole argument. The debt came first. The tax is Parliament's answer to the debt, not the other way round' became 'Keep the order straight: the debt came first, and the tax is Parliament's answer to it, not the other way round'. Same proposition, same anti-reversal guard, seven fewer words. The card is 79 words before and after, and the deck is unchanged at 180.9 seconds.
reinstated.whatItDoesNotDo: It does not widen any duel rubric. WHAT_IT_LEFT already accepted any financial answer, so 'they had an army to pay for over here' was correct before the module said it and is correct now; it is added to that item's accept list so the connection is visible. Territory named without a cost — 'they got Canada' — is still wrong, because the item asks what Parliament is solving and land is not a bill.

deliberateExclusions.content: Stamp duties payable in scarce hard coin.
deliberateExclusions.why: Real, and TEA's own 2023 rubric accepts it, but nothing in the eighteen items asks for it. The module is 1:1 with the duel: content no item asks for is three minutes spent on something the mission does not test.

deliberateExclusions.content: Andrew Oliver, his effigy, the Liberty Tree, and the Loyal Nine — the actual events of 14 August 1765.
deliberateExclusions.why: The most tempting cut of all, because the module is dated the day it happened and the story is better than anything here. They are MICRO enrichment in the curriculum registry, no duel item asks for them, and each one costs eight to ten seconds of a hard budget. They belong in the reactive world or the Codex, not in the mission's preparation.
A named clause of 8.4(A) and a live gap in the registry, but M1 does not own it and no M1 item asks for it.

engagementDecisions: Second person throughout, and the reader is a runner rather than a student. The identity card gives them a job in the first eight words.
Every abstraction is spent immediately on something physical: the deed and the bolt of cloth, the barrel of nails, the letter in a woman's own hand, three pence against a farthing.
The two frame cards are the stakes. The last line of the deck is the constable saying he will ask, which is literally true — the six questions are the next thing that happens.

The cognitive load is deliberate and is concentrated in three sentences: the order of debt and tax, the boundary between paper and goods, and the difference between a lawful vote and consent. Those three are the hard part of the chapter and the module says so rather than smoothing them.

The primary source is the payoff of the synthesis card rather than decoration. A student reads Parliament calling it 'just and necessary' to raise a revenue in America after having just been told the debt came first, and the two halves meet.
